strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful question: whether stable feature-learning parameterisations leave predictive coding meaningfully different from backpropagation at scale. The equilibrated-energy formulation gives an intuitive explanation for why increasing width can suppress their differences.

Originality: The proposed characterisation of admissible parameterisations and extension to joint width–depth scaling go beyond merely exhibiting a parameterisation where PC approximates BP. Appendix A.2 clearly distinguishes these intended contributions from Ishikawa et al. (2024) and Innocenti et al. (2025).

Evidence: Figures 1–3 and the supplementary experiments systematically vary width and depth, compare energy rescaling and gradient alignment, and include direct loss-trajectory comparisons. Experiments with nonlinear MLPs, CNNs, and transformers provide useful evidence beyond the linear setting.

Presentation and limitations: The main exposition is clear and well organised. Section 6.3 candidly discusses linearity, inference cost, short training runs, and attention locality. These disclosures are valuable, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—necessity is not established: In Appendix A.4, the transition from Eq. 65 to Eqs. 66–67 requires every layer's contribution to prediction evolution to remain order one. The stated Desideratum 2 only requires their sum to remain order one. Likewise, features can change through earlier layers even if a layer's own weight contribution vanishes, as Eq. 89 explicitly shows. The derivation therefore imposes stronger conditions than the stated desiderata, undermining the central claim that Eq. 15 exhausts all admissible parameterisations.

Soundness—Theorem 2 has a consequential gap: Eqs. 120–121 retain the first-layer feature derivative, but it disappears in Eqs. 122–123. In the regime N much larger than L, this term can remain order one for alpha greater than 1/2 and propagate through near-identity residual blocks. Thus, vanishing residual-branch contributions do not by themselves violate the stated Desideratum 5. Additionally, Eq. 122 substitutes denominators involving 1 + N^(-1), although Eq. 107 gives s = 1 + Theta(L/N), and Eq. 120 drops an accumulated propagation term without a bound. The claimed unique depth exponent needs stronger assumptions and a revised derivation.

Soundness—extension throughout training is insufficiently justified: The norm calculations in Eqs. 45–47 and 104–107 use random-initialisation statistics, but the conclusions are asserted throughout feature-learning dynamics, when weights become correlated. The manuscript does not establish the necessary time-uniform control of these norms or their derivatives. Convergence of energy values alone also does not establish convergence of gradients. A precise convergence mode, training-time interval, joint-limit regime, and control of the gradient correction in Eq. 26 are needed.

Empirical support: Figure 4 primarily reports whole-network gradient cosine similarity for representative runs over 100 updates. Alignment does not establish agreement in gradient magnitude or in every layer, and can conceal discrepancies in layers contributing little to the total norm. Relative gradient errors, layerwise comparisons, quantified activity-stationarity residuals, and variability across seeds would more directly test the claimed equivalence.

Significance and scope: Appendix A.8 reports that layer normalisation breaks the observed PC-to-BP convergence even at large width, so it was removed from the transformer. This important boundary should be prominent in the main claims about nonlinear architectures and modern language models. The short ImageNet and character-level experiments support a restricted correspondence observation, not demonstrated scalable training or computational advantage; the deepest nonlinear MLP requires 100,000 inference iterations per update.

Reproducibility: Appendix A.8 supplies useful hyperparameters, but inference convergence is asserted from fixed iteration budgets without a numerical stopping criterion or residual measurements. The supplied manuscript also leaves the promised code location blank in Sections 5 and A.8. These omissions make the equilibrium-dependent empirical claims difficult to verify.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful theoretical question: whether predictive coding admits stable, feature-learning parameterisations distinct from backpropagation. Connecting this question to the equilibrated-energy rescaling provides an interpretable explanation for why wide PC networks can approach BP.

Originality: The proposed characterisation of admissible parameterisations and extension to joint width/depth scaling go beyond simply exhibiting one PC parameterisation that approximates BP. Section A.2 clearly identifies the intended advances over Ishikawa et al. (2024) and Innocenti et al. (2025).

Empirical evidence: The experiments cover linear networks, nonlinear residual MLPs, CNNs, and transformers. Width/depth sweeps, energy-rescaling measurements, and comparisons with the standard parameterisation provide useful evidence for the proposed correspondence in the tested settings.

Presentation and limitations: The main exposition is generally clear, with explicit desiderata and helpful summaries. Section 6.3 candidly acknowledges linear theory, expensive inference, short training runs, and nonlocal attention. The work raises no apparent material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—depth uniqueness is not established under the stated desiderata. In A.5.3, Eqs. 120–121 retain the contribution dh^(1)/dt, but Eq. 122 drops it when concluding that alpha = 1/2 is necessary. With trainable input weights, this contribution can remain order one and propagate through near-identity residual layers even when alpha > 1/2. Thus, order-one total feature evolution does not by itself require nonvanishing contributions from the residual weights. The argument needs a stronger desideratum concerning residual-branch learning or a revised uniqueness claim. This directly affects Theorem 2 and the central 'only scalable parameterisation' conclusion.

Soundness—the joint-limit calculation contains unresolved approximations. Equation 107 gives s(theta) = 1 + Theta(L/N), whereas Eq. 122 uses denominators containing 1 + N^(-1), losing the depth dependence. Additionally, the propagation term in Eq. 119 is discarded as higher order without controlling its accumulation across L layers. These steps require an explicit limit regime and error bounds; they do not presently justify the unrestricted depth-stability theorem.

Soundness—the claimed throughout-training extension needs additional justification. The norm calculations in Eqs. 45–47 and 104–107 rely on initialisation-based moment and forward-stability arguments, but no corresponding control of the learned weight products over training is established. Initialisation scaling alone does not imply these estimates persist after weights become correlated. Likewise, convergence of objective values is insufficient to establish convergence of gradients; the corollaries need a specified gradient norm and control of both the rescaling derivative and its effect under the width-dependent learning rate.

Evaluation and reproducibility: Figure 4 principally reports global gradient cosine similarity, which cannot establish agreement in gradient magnitude and may hide discrepancies in individual layers. The experiments should also report relative gradient errors and layerwise comparisons. Although A.8 supplies architectures, learning rates, batch sizes, and inference budgets, it gives no quantitative stationarity criterion demonstrating that the required activity equilibrium was reached. Representative runs and statements that seeds behaved similarly provide limited uncertainty information for this central empirical claim.

Significance and scope: The nonlinear results support a narrower conclusion than the assertion that the linear theory 'remains valid for nonlinear models.' The main practical experiments run for only 100 weight updates, and A.8 reports that layer normalisation broke PC–BP convergence and was therefore removed from the transformer. This failure should be investigated and foregrounded when discussing modern language models. The disclosed requirement of up to 100,000 inference iterations also means these experiments establish short-horizon correspondence, not practical scalability or computational advantage. These limitations are honestly acknowledged, but the broader claims still exceed the evidence.

strengths: Significance: Understanding which parameterisations permit stable predictive-coding training is a useful research question. The connection between the equilibrated energy, mean-field scaling, and the width-to-depth ratio provides a potentially valuable explanation of when PC approaches backpropagation.

Originality: The intended contribution goes beyond earlier existence results by attempting to characterise necessary parameterisation conditions and extend the analysis to depth and training dynamics. This is a meaningful conceptual direction, even though the necessity claims need correction.

Empirical evidence: The width/depth sweeps, standard-parameterisation comparisons, and nonlinear experiments provide consistent evidence for increasing PC–BP gradient alignment in the tested regimes. Evaluating both analytic equilibrated energies and numerical activity inference helps distinguish the theoretical mechanism from inference failures.

Presentation and limitations: The main narrative is clear, with explicit desiderata, informative figures, and extensive derivations. Section 6.3 candidly discusses linearity, inference cost, short training horizons, and attention locality. The theoretical study presents no apparent material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—width uniqueness is not established by the stated desiderata. In Appendix A.4.3, Eqs. 65–67 require every layer's contribution to the prediction dynamics to be order one, although Desideratum 2 only requires their sum to be order one. Likewise, Eq. 89 includes feature changes inherited from preceding layers, so order-one feature evolution does not require an order-one direct update from each layer's own weights. The proof therefore imposes stronger conditions than those stated. This undermines the central claim that the derived family is the only admissible family; a maximal direct-update condition or a different necessity argument is needed.

Soundness—Theorem 2 has a related concrete gap. Eqs. 120–121 retain the input-layer contribution dh^(1)/dt, but it disappears in Eqs. 122–123 when concluding that alpha = 1/2 is necessary. For alpha > 1/2, residual contributions can vanish while the trainable input layer still produces order-one feature evolution through the identity paths. Desideratum 5, as written, does not exclude this case. The proof needs to distinguish nontrivial learning by residual branches from nontrivial evolution of the total features.

Soundness—the joint-limit and throughout-training claims require additional control. Eq. 107 gives s = 1 + Θ(L/N), but Eq. 122 uses denominators involving 1 + N^(-1), losing the depth dependence without specifying a limiting regime. Moreover, several path-norm estimates originate from independent Gaussian initialisation and are subsequently used during training without establishing the required bounds for correlated, trained weights. Explicit limit ordering, training-time assumptions, and control of the derivative correction in Eq. 26 are needed to substantiate the claimed gradient equivalence throughout training.

Evaluation and significance: Figure 4 primarily measures cosine similarity over 100 updates. Alignment alone does not establish equality of gradient magnitudes or learning trajectories. Relative gradient errors, layerwise comparisons, and activity-stationarity residuals would more directly test the claims. Appendix A.8 also reports that layer normalisation breaks the observed correspondence and was removed from the transformer; this important qualification should accompany the main-text assertion that the linear theory remains valid for nonlinear models.

Practical scope and reproducibility: The reported inference budgets reach 100,000 iterations per update, and competitive end-to-end training or hyperparameter transfer is not demonstrated. These are honestly acknowledged limitations, but they leave the broader claims about implementing BP at scale prospective. Although architecture descriptions and many hyperparameters are supplied, numerical equilibrium tolerances, quantitative seed variability for Figure 4, and complete optimiser settings would improve reproducibility. Overall, the promising mechanism and empirical trends do not compensate for unresolved gaps in the central necessity theorems.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful question: which parameterisations permit stable feature learning in predictive coding as width and depth increase? Connecting this question to backpropagation could clarify when PC offers distinct learning dynamics.

Originality: The joint width–depth analysis and proposed O(L/N) gradient correspondence extend the prior existence and initialisation results discussed in Appendix A.2. The equilibrated-energy formulation provides an informative explanation of the correspondence.

Empirical evidence: The width/depth sweeps and experiments spanning linear networks, nonlinear MLPs, CNNs, and transformers consistently support increasing gradient alignment in the tested settings. Separating exact equilibrated-energy experiments from iterative inference experiments is helpful.

Presentation and ethics: The main exposition is clear, with explicit desiderata and extensive derivations. Section 6.3 candidly discusses linearity, inference cost, short training horizons, and attention locality. There are no apparent material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—central uniqueness claim: The transition from Eq. 64 to Eqs. 65–66 requires every layer's kernel contribution to be order one, although Desideratum 2 only requires their sum to be order one. Likewise, Desideratum 3 concerns total feature evolution, which can arise from updates in earlier layers even when a layer's own direct update vanishes. For example, for one hidden layer, choosing a1=b1=c=0, d=1/2, a2=1, and b2=-1 preserves the usual forward scaling and permits order-one hidden-feature and prediction updates through the input weights, while the readout's direct contribution vanishes. This lies outside Eq. 15 but satisfies the stated scaling desiderata for nondegenerate data. The proof therefore needs an additional maximal-direct-update requirement or a weaker conclusion. This undermines the claimed necessity that distinguishes the work from prior results.

Soundness—training-time and joint-limit guarantees: Appendix A.4 derives product-norm scalings using independent initial weights (Eq. 47), then uses such scalings to support claims throughout training without establishing their preservation under PC dynamics. Appendix A.6 additionally assumes uniform layerwise relative-error bounds in Eq. 146; these do not follow merely from a non-vanishing complete MSE gradient. The corollaries need precise probabilistic statements, training-time scope, and justified uniform bounds on path products and gradient nondegeneracy.

Evaluation: Figure 4 primarily measures cosine similarity. This cannot establish equality of gradient magnitudes or the relative-error convergence claimed in Eqs. 16 and 20, and a concatenated cosine can conceal discrepancies in individual layers. Layerwise relative errors, gradient-norm ratios, quantitative inference residuals, and measured convergence rates would directly test the claims. Representative runs without uncertainty estimates further limit this evidence.

Significance and scope: The nonlinear demonstrations cover only 100 training steps and do not establish successful large-scale training or hyperparameter transfer. More consequentially, Appendix A.9 reports that layer normalization breaks the transformer correspondence even at large width, motivating its removal. This material boundary should be prominent in the main experimental conclusions. The acknowledged need for up to 100,000 inference iterations also leaves practical scalability unestablished; acknowledging this limitation is appropriate, but the stronger implementation-at-scale implications remain speculative.

Reproducibility: Appendices A.7–A.9 provide useful architecture and optimisation details, but the submitted manuscript's code-availability statements contain no usable repository link. Activity initialisation and quantitative equilibrium criteria are insufficiently specified despite their importance to the results. The transformer equations also warrant clarification: Eq. 156 uses unscaled Q/K/V projections while stating standard-Gaussian initialisation, making the intended width scaling difficult to reconstruct.

strengths: Significance and originality: Connecting predictive-coding parameterisations to feature learning and PC–BP gradient agreement is useful. The joint width–depth analysis and proposed O(L/N) gradient discrepancy extend the prior existence and initialisation results discussed in Appendix A.2.

Soundness: The exact linear-network identity F*=L/s provides a clear analytical foundation. Differentiating this identity exposes both sources of gradient discrepancy, and the width/depth sweeps support the predicted behaviour of the rescaling factor.

Presentation: The main text clearly introduces the parameterisation, desiderata, and relationship between the theoretical and numerical settings. The appendices provide substantial derivations, architecture descriptions, and experimental hyperparameters.

Limitations and ethics: The authors candidly acknowledge linearity, inference cost, short training runs, and nonlocal transformer attention. These disclosures are valuable, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central uniqueness claim: Appendix A.4.3 moves from requiring the sum of layer contributions in Eq. 64 to be Θ(1) to requiring every contribution to be Θ(1), yielding Eqs. 65–66. The stated prediction-stability desideratum does not require this stronger condition. Likewise, hidden features can evolve through updates in preceding layers even when their own layer's direct update vanishes. Consequently, the derivation does not establish that Eq. 15 exhausts all parameterisations satisfying the stated desiderata. This directly undermines the necessity claim highlighted as the main advance over Ishikawa et al.

Soundness—convergence throughout training: The path-norm estimates in Eqs. 47–49 and 108–115 rely on initialisation calculations and asserted stability, without establishing the required bounds along trained, correlated trajectories. Appendix A.6 additionally assumes typical Θ-scalings for each layer's MSE gradient and a uniform layerwise relative-error bound in Eq. 146. A non-vanishing complete gradient, as stated in the corollaries, does not itself supply these assumptions. The claimed training-time convergence rates need explicit non-degeneracy conditions and bounds uniform in depth and over a specified training interval.

Evaluation: Figure 4 principally measures cosine similarity, which cannot establish convergence in gradient magnitude or verify the claimed relative-error rates. Quantitative inference residuals, gradient-norm ratios, and layerwise relative errors are missing. Fixed budgets of 200, 800, or 100,000 inference iterations do not by themselves establish equilibrium, particularly when the conclusion is conditional on equilibrium being reached.

Significance and scope: Appendix A.9 reports that layer normalisation breaks PC–BP convergence even at large width and was therefore removed from the transformer experiment. This is an important boundary of the claimed practical generality and deserves prominent analysis. The 100-step practical experiments also do not establish competitive task performance, hyperparameter transfer, or computational scalability; the acknowledged inference costs make those broader implications prospective.

Reproducibility: Although many settings are documented, activity initialisation and quantitative convergence criteria are insufficiently specified. Figure 4 reports representative runs with only a qualitative assertion of consistency across seeds. Additionally, Eqs. 155–156 omit width normalisation for the query/key/value projections while specifying standard-Gaussian weights; as written, these projections do not have width-stable variance. Clarifying the implemented attention scalings is necessary to reproduce and interpret this experiment.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful question: which parameterisations allow predictive coding (PC) to remain stable and learn features as networks grow? Connecting this question to PC–backpropagation (BP) equivalence provides potentially valuable guidance for scaling PC.

Originality: The joint width–depth analysis and proposed O(L/N) relative gradient discrepancy extend the fixed-width/depth correspondences discussed in prior work. The contribution is primarily new understanding rather than a new training algorithm.

Evidence: The linear experiments examine energy rescaling, losses, and gradient alignment across widths and depths. Experiments with nonlinear MLPs, CNNs, and transformers provide additional evidence that alignment can extend beyond the theoretical setting.

Presentation and ethics: The main exposition is well organised, with explicit desiderata and extensive derivations. Section 6.3 candidly discusses linearity, inference costs, incomplete training, and attention locality. These disclosures are valuable, and I see no material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—necessity is not established under the stated desiderata. In Appendix A.4.3, Eqs. 64–66 require each layer's contribution to the prediction update to be order one, although Desideratum 2 only requires the total update to be order one. Likewise, Desideratum 3 concerns total feature evolution, which can be inherited from earlier layers even when a layer's own weight update is subleading (Eq. 89). For example, in a three-layer network, choosing a=(0,1,1/2), b=(0,-1,0), c=0, d=1/2 preserves standard effective initialisation and allows order-one feature evolution through the first layer while suppressing the middle layer's direct update. This falls outside Eq. 15. The paper needs an explicit maximal-direct-update condition or a weaker conclusion. This matters because necessity is presented as a principal advance over Ishikawa et al. (2024).

Soundness—training-time convergence requires additional justification. Appendices A.4–A.6 carry initialisation-based norm and component estimates into training without establishing their preservation along PC trajectories. In the joint limit, the gradient argument additionally needs bounds uniform over the growing number of layers; Eq. 146 assumes such a bound. Non-vanishing of the complete MSE gradient alone does not establish the layerwise lower bounds used in Eqs. 134–144. The corollaries should state precise time, probabilistic, and non-degeneracy assumptions and justify the corresponding uniform estimates.

Experimental support: Figure 4 primarily measures cosine similarity, which establishes directional alignment but not relative gradient convergence or matching update magnitudes. It therefore does not directly validate the stronger convergence language in Takeaway 4. Relative gradient errors, layerwise comparisons, and measured inference residuals would distinguish finite-inference effects from the predicted width scaling. Representative runs without uncertainty estimates further limit assessment.

Practical significance is narrower than the broad scaling claims suggest. The main nonlinear experiments run for only 100 weight updates, with up to 100,000 inference iterations per update for residual MLPs. Appendix A.9 also reports that layer normalisation breaks the observed PC–BP convergence and was removed from the transformer. These honestly reported findings do not invalidate the restricted theory, but they substantially limit conclusions about standard transformers or practical implementation of BP at scale.

Reproducibility: The supplied manuscript has blank code-availability locations in both Section 5 and Appendix A.9. Although many hyperparameters are documented, inference initialisation and quantitative convergence criteria are not adequately specified. The transformer equations also require clarification: Eq. 156 shows unnormalised Q/K/V projections while the text specifies standard-Gaussian initialisation for all weights, making the intended width scaling difficult to reconstruct. Together with the central theoretical gaps, these issues prevent acceptance in the current form.
